subject: Business
title: The Containerization Revolution
description: Learn The Containerization Revolution in one minute.

hook.text: Before 1956, loading a ship took weeks. Longshoremen carried cargo piece by piece. Then the shipping container arrived.

buildup.text: Malcom McLean invented the standardized container: a metal box that fits on ships, trains, and trucks interchangeably.

discovery.text: Loading time dropped from days to hours. Shipping costs fell 90%. Global trade became economically viable.

twist.text: The container didn't just change shipping. It enabled globalization. Manufacturing could now be done anywhere cheaply.

climax.text: Today, 90% of world trade moves in containers. The humble metal box reshaped the global economy.

punchline.text: The most transformative invention in trade isn't a technology. It's a box.

quiz.question: How much did containerization reduce shipping costs?

details.summary: Containerization transformed global trade by standardizing cargo into uniform steel boxes that transfer seamlessly between ships, trucks, and trains. Introduced by Malcom McLean in 1956, it slashed shipping costs by over 90 percent and enabled modern globalization.

faq.question: How did containerization reduce shipping costs so dramatically?
faq.answer: Before containers, cargo was loaded piece by piece, taking days and requiring large dock crews. Standard containers are loaded at the factory, sealed, and transferred between ships, trucks, and trains without opening. This reduced port time from weeks to hours.

faq.question: What are the standard container sizes used globally?
faq.answer: The most common sizes are 20-foot and 40-foot containers, standardized by the International Organization for Standardization. A TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit) is the standard measure of container capacity. Modern container ships carry over 20,000 TEUs.
